newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia's Ung Huot seen as having calming effect.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia's Ung Huot seen as having calming effect.

text.p: Cambodian Foreign Minister Ung Huot, chosen by parliament on Wednesday to replace ousted Prince Norodom Ranariddh as first prime minister, is a likeable and able politician who should have a calming influence on the country's turbulent politics, analysts said.
But the 52-year-old moderate faces a huge task in rebuilding the shattered royalist FUNCINPEC party and preparing for elections next year.
"He'll be the acceptable face of the government. He'll play a calming role, he won't be as provocative as Ranariddh," said a diplomat. "He's not in it for the fight."

More than two thirds of the members of the 120-seat National Assembly voted in favour of Ung Huot's nomination to replace Ranariddh, who was ousted by his co-premier Hun Sen in a bloody takeover a month ago.
"He's an affable person, easy to talk to and he also has a good mind," said an Asian diplomat.

Ung Huot rose to prominence as the director of FUNCINPEC's successful 1993 election campaign, but analysts said he would have his work cut out if he hopes to repeat the performance in elections scheduled for May.

"I can't see how the party can run an effective election campaign whoever heads it," said a Western diplomat. "It's been bruised, its headquarters have been trashed. The party has effectively been dismantled."
"He has to rebuild the party, but that requires the blessing of the people outside the country," said the Asian diplomat, referring to Ranariddh and other senior royalists who fled last month.
"A lot of people have goodwill towards Ung Huot. The question is whether he can overcome Ranariddh's disapproval."
Ung Huot became foreign minister in October 1994, replacing Prince Norodom Sirivudh, who resigned to protest the ouster of the outspoken Sam Rainsy as Minister of Finance.
Before his career in politics, Ung Huot spent more than two decades in Australia where he received a master's degree in business administration from Melbourne University in 1974.

He decided not to return to Cambodia after finishing his studies. At the time the country was in turmoil as the Khmer Rouge guerrilla group, architects of the 1975-79 "killing fields" rein of terror, tightened their noose on the capital, Phnom Penh.
Staying in Australia, he worked his way up the ranks of Telecom Australia over 17 years, from clerk to marketing executive, and in the 1980s he began working for FUNCINPEC party in Australia.
In 1992, he returned to Cambodia to steer FUNCINPEC to its election victory the following year. He was elected to parliament representing a seat in his home province, Kandal.
He became education minister in the new coalition government and gained a reputation for integrity as a result of his efforts to curb teacher bribes and exam cheating.
At the foreign ministry he spearheaded efforts to gain the country's entry to the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) which was postponed after last month's coup.
He said recently he would retain his post as foreign minister and is expected to continue to devote much of his time to foreign affairs.
He will also have to face some opposition to his nomination to replace Ranariddh, whose father, King Norodom Sihanouk, said last month the post still belonged to his son.
The Cambodian constitution requires the king's approval of a new first prime minister.
